title: Split reductive neutral model from a reductive special neutral fibre
statement: Let $R$ be a henselian discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring, def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology] with algebraically closed residue field $F$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure] and fraction field $L$. Let $\mathcal N$ be a smooth affine finite-type $R$-group scheme with geometrically connected generic fibre. Group schemes over a ring have multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams of [def-sc-group-scheme], with that ring as base. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Assume the identity component $\mathcal N_F^0$ of the special fibre is reductive. Over a field, reductive means smooth, geometrically connected, affine of finite type, with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup after algebraic closure; unipotent means that all geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful representation. The union of $\mathcal N_L$ and $\mathcal N_F^0$ in $|\mathcal N|$, with its induced open-subscheme structure [def-weil-open-immersion], is an open affine finite-type subgroup scheme $\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal N$. It satisfies $\mathcal D_L=\mathcal N_L$ and $\mathcal D_F=\mathcal N_F^0$, and is split reductive over $R$: it is smooth affine of finite type with reductive geometric fibres and admits a closed subgroup scheme $\mathcal T\cong\mathbf G_{m,R}^{r}$ which is a maximal torus in every geometric fibre. Here $\mathbf G_{m,R}=\operatorname{Spec}R[t,t^{-1}]$ with multiplication of units, a torus over an algebraically closed field is a group isomorphic to a finite product of $\mathbf G_m$, and maximal means maximal under subgroup inclusion. The integer $r\geq0$ is allowed to be zero.

source.place: WANTED locally; read online https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0405381: Lemma 3.5 and Section 3.6, followed by Proposition 4.3, first paragraph of proof, printed pp.6-8: apply the neutral-component argument to the smooth model, after its special neutral fibre has been shown reductive

proof.text: Put $H=\mathcal N_F^0$. By [lem-sfb-finite-type-group-identity-subgroup], $H$ is an open and closed subgroup scheme of $\mathcal N_F$. Its complement is closed in the closed special fibre, hence closed in $\mathcal N$. Remove that complement and call the resulting open subscheme $\mathcal D$. Its generic fibre is $\mathcal N_L$ and its special fibre is $H$, as schemes. Multiplication on $\mathcal D\times_R\mathcal D$, inversion on $\mathcal D$, and the identity have image in this open: over $L$ there is nothing removed, and over $F$ this follows from the subgroup property of $H$. A morphism whose image lies in an open factors uniquely through its restricted structure sheaf. The restricted maps satisfy the group diagrams since they do so after the open immersion into $\mathcal N$. Thus $\mathcal D$ is the specified open subgroup.

source.place: Lemma 3.5 and the neutral-component paragraph preceding it, printed p.6; Stacks Tag 0B7R (groupoids-proposition-connected-component)

proof.text: Write $\mathcal N=\operatorname{Spec}E$ and choose a uniformizer $\pi$ of $R$. The smooth affine comparison [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map-iff-smooth-affine] makes $E$ a smooth $R$-algebra. By [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map-flat] it is flat, and [lem-trf-flat-module-torsionfree-domain] makes multiplication by $\pi$ injective. Thus $E\subset E[1/\pi]$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-spec-clopen-idempotent] to the complement of $H$ in $\operatorname{Spec}(E/\pi E)$: obtain $\bar a^2=\bar a$ with $H=V(\bar a)=D(1-\bar a)$. Choose a lift $a\in E$ and $b\in E$ satisfying $a(1-a)=\pi b$. Then $|\mathcal D|=D_E(\pi)\cup D_E(1-a)$.

source.place: Lemma 3.5, alternative affine-dilatation argument, printed p.6; algebraic charts written out here; Stacks Tags 00TA, 00SL, 00EE

proof.text: Put $t=a/\pi$ and $B=E[t]\subset E[1/\pi]$. In $B$, $1=(1-a)+\pi t$, so the basic opens $D_B(\pi)$ and $D_B(1-a)$ cover $\operatorname{Spec}B$. The corresponding ring maps are isomorphisms: $B[1/\pi]=E[1/\pi]$, and $B[1/(1-a)]=E[1/(1-a)]$ because $t=b/(1-a)$ there. The latter equality holds inside $E[1/\pi,1/(1-a)]$, into which $E[1/(1-a)]$ injects by the preceding torsion-freeness. By [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-section-vanishing-prime], these are exactly the maps on the two basic-open charts of $\operatorname{Spec}E$; hence $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}E$ identifies its charts, and their common localization, with $D_E(\pi)$ and $D_E(1-a)$. This identifies $\mathcal D=\operatorname{Spec}B$. In particular it is affine of finite type over $R$, since $E$ is finitely generated and only $t$ is adjoined.

source.place: Lemma 3.5, alternative argument: explicit coordinate version of the affine dilatation; Stacks Tag 01I3 (schemes-lemma-standard-open-affine)

proof.text: By [lem-pc-open-immersion-smooth-composition], $\mathcal D$ is smooth over $R$. Apply the first assertion of [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-fibre-openness] to $\mathcal D$ at the closed point of $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$. Its geometric special fibre is $H$, reductive by hypothesis because $F$ is algebraically closed. The required finite presentation follows from smoothness and affineness by [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map-iff-smooth-affine]. Every open neighborhood of the closed point of this local spectrum is all of $S$: a basic open containing the maximal ideal is defined by a unit. Thus all geometric fibre identity components of $\mathcal D$ are reductive. Its geometric generic fibre is connected by the hypothesis on $\mathcal N_L$, and its special fibre is the connected $H$. Therefore the geometric fibres themselves are reductive.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.9(1), printed pp.85-88; Prasad--Yu Proposition 4.3 first paragraph; Stacks Tags 01VC, 01VA

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], choose a split maximal torus $T_0\simeq\mathbf G_{m,F}^r$ in $H$. Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-etale-subgroup-lift] to the smooth affine $R$-group $\mathcal D$, its closed point, and this immersion. Obtain $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ etale over $S$, an $F$-point $u$ above the closed point, and $j:\mathbf G_{m,U}^r\hookrightarrow\mathcal D_U$. Since etale morphisms are smooth [lem-weil-pbc-etale-smooth-zero-dimensional-fibres], [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map-iff-smooth-affine] makes $C$ a smooth $R$-algebra. Apply [lem-trf-henselian-smooth-algebra-lifting] with base ring $R$, target algebra $R$ and ideal $(\pi)$ to the residue map $C\to F$ of $u$. The maximal-ideal pair is henselian by hypothesis. Obtain $C\to R$ lifting it, equivalently a section $S\to U$ through $u$. Pulling back $j$ along that section gives a closed subgroup $\mathcal T\simeq\mathbf G_{m,R}^r$ in $\mathcal D$, with special fibre $T_0$. On coordinate rings a closed immersion is a quotient, and tensoring this quotient with $R$ is again a quotient, so the pulled-back immersion is closed.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.6, printed pp.83-84, and Proposition B.3.4, printed pp.290-292; Stacks Tag 0H74 (more-algebra-lemma-lift-smooth-henselian)

proof.text: Apply the second assertion of [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-fibre-openness] to $\mathcal D$ and $\mathcal T$. The special fibre is reductive and $T_0$ is maximal there by the preceding choice. It follows that $\mathcal T$ is maximal on all geometric fibres over an open neighborhood of the closed point, hence over all of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ by the unit argument in Step 4. Along with Steps 1, 3 and 4 this proves every required assertion, including the rank-zero case.

proof_origin.place: Lemma 3.5 and Proposition 4.3 first paragraph, with Conrad Propositions 3.1.6, 3.1.9 and B.3.4 as generic tools, read online; both local copies WANTED. Explicit localization and henselian-section assembly by Q13.
